title: What Homer’s ‘Odyssey’ Tells Us About the Economics of the Bronze Age
gist: Adam Tooze reads the Odyssey as economic history: Bronze Age great-power economics revolved around the copper and tin trade, with Troy likely a toll-taker on tin shipments to Mycenaean Greece before war, dysfunctional economic structures and climate change collapsed every eastern Mediterranean civilization except Egypt. He then maps ancient risk management onto modern monetary policy, arguing the Odysseus-and-the-sirens self-binding story is an explicitly conservative myth about central bank independence — and flags that new Fed chair Kevin Warsh opposes the softer 'Delphic' forward-guidance alternative.

themes.theme: Bronze Age commodity geopolitics and the tin chokepoint

insights.claim: Bronze Age great-power economics in the eastern Mediterranean revolved around trade in copper and tin, with copper relatively abundant while tin had to be shipped from as far away as Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: The oldest documented great-power economy was organized around a single scarce, long-haul input — the original template for today's critical-minerals chokepoint analysis.
insights.locator: And the key commodity is bronze

insights.claim: Troy's economy was most likely based on toll-taking on shipments of tin bound for the Mycenaean Greek states, making the Trojan War a conflict over a trade chokepoint rather than only a dynastic quarrel.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Rent extraction at a maritime chokepoint has been a casus belli for 3,000 years — the same logic that makes Hormuz, Suez and Malacca strategic today.
insights.quote: which was basically a kind of toll-taking on shipments of tin to the Mycenaean Greek states
insights.locator: And that’s what we think the economy of Troy

insights.claim: The Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean hosted multiple large-scale imperial state structures simultaneously — Egypt, the Hittites in central Turkey, the Mycenaean Greek statelets and the Babylonians.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A genuinely multipolar interconnected system existed and then collapsed wholesale — relevant precedent for systemic rather than local geopolitical risk.
insights.locator: Egypt’s still there from much, much earlier

themes.theme: The Late Bronze Age collapse as multi-causal systemic failure

insights.claim: From the early 1200s through the mid-1100s B.C. a total catastrophe hit eastern Mediterranean civilizations — the great crisis of the Bronze Age — out of which only Egypt survived while all other state structures were massively disrupted.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A near-total civilizational wipeout with one survivor is the base case for how interconnected systems fail — not gradual decline but correlated collapse.
insights.quote: a total catastrophe hits the eastern Mediterranean civilizations. It’s known as the great crisis of the Bronze Age, out of which only Egypt survived.
insights.locator: And from the early 1200s through to the mid-1100s B.C.

insights.claim: The Bronze Age collapse is attributed to a combination of warmaking, dysfunctional economic structures and climate change, which together had destroyed all the major civilizations of the era by the 1100s B.C.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: War plus structural economic fragility plus climate shock is a named historical failure combination — a checklist worth applying to present-day stress cases.
insights.quote: And we think it’s an effect of warmaking, various types of dysfunctional economic structure, and of climate change
insights.locator: And so, Homer’s epic is looking back

insights.claim: Homer's epics date to roughly 800 B.C. and describe events around 1200 B.C., a 400-year gap equivalent to writing poetry in 2020 about events under Charlemagne, and classical Greece with Athens and Sparta came 400 years after Homer.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: The founding text of Western civilization is itself a distant reconstruction — a caution about how much economic detail any long-memory narrative can carry.
insights.quote: So this is as though we were, in a complicated, arcane, poetic way, writing poetry in 2020 about stuff that happened under Charlemagne.
insights.locator: The crucial thing to realize

insights.claim: The Odyssey functions as the foundational shock narrative of Western civilization because it looks back not only at the disaster of a war but at a civilization already on the cusp of disintegration.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Western economic and political storytelling is anchored in collapse, not in growth — which shapes how the culture frames risk.
insights.locator: So it’s not for nothing in Western civilization

themes.theme: Oikos, autarky and the division of labor

insights.claim: The English word 'economy' derives from the Greek oikos meaning household, and the Bronze Age palace economies were simply super oikoi — the large households that drove long-distance trade.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Economics originated as household management scaled up, which is why sovereign and family balance-sheet metaphors keep recurring in policy debate.
insights.locator: The big drivers of the economy in the Bronze Age

insights.claim: The Greek word autarky, meaning economic self-sufficiency, originates in the oikos, whose defining function was to be a relatively self-sufficient unit of integrated economic management and material production.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Self-sufficiency is not a modern nationalist invention but the original organizing goal of the economic unit — useful framing for today's reshoring debate.
insights.quote: it’s not by accident that the word for economic self-sufficiency, autarky, is also Greek
insights.locator: And it’s not by accident that the word

insights.claim: The oikos achieved self-sufficiency through division of labor, with tasks allocated by gender and by free-versus-slave status, making it a social organism rather than an undifferentiated unit.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Division of labor predates markets — specialization emerged inside the household long before it was priced.
insights.locator: And it achieves that through a second fundamental principle

insights.claim: The domestic plot of the Odyssey — who will marry the supposed widow — is fundamentally a contest over control of the oikos, making it a property and management succession story.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: The West's oldest domestic drama is a corporate control fight; marriage as an ownership-transfer mechanism.
insights.quote: Who’s going to end up marrying the widow, the supposed widow?
insights.locator: And that, after all, is the central question

themes.theme: Hesiod's iron age: a meta-theory of risk

insights.claim: Hesiod, a farmer writing Works and Days in the 8th century B.C., built a historical narrative of five generations — golden, silver, bronze, the heroic age that died at Troy, and the present iron generation — to explain why the world is risky.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: The earliest Western risk model is a declension narrative — risk explained by moral history rather than by probability.
insights.locator: There’s a source, a farmer named Hesiod

insights.claim: Hesiod's iron generation is defined by a weather system of alternating pain and joy that must be prudently managed, from which he derives the practical instruction to build granaries because summer will not last forever.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Buffer stocks and reserves as the original answer to cyclical uncertainty — precautionary saving predates finance by three millennia.
insights.quote: Summer won’t last forever, so what have you got to do? You’ve got to build granaries.
insights.locator: And in that world, to live free of worries

insights.claim: Because Greek cosmology placed outcomes in the hands of capricious gods, risk mitigation took the form of divination — the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi for those who could afford it, dice throwing for those who could not — rather than any pooling or insurance mechanism.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Where uncertainty is attributed to agency rather than distribution, forecasting substitutes for hedging — the same instinct that drives markets to over-consume central bank guidance.
insights.locator: So what can you do?

insights.claim: The Greeks were the great originator in the Western tradition of games of luck, which functioned not only as entertainment but as means of divination.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Randomization began as an information-gathering ritual, not a probability exercise — the pre-history of quantified risk.
insights.quote: The Greeks were, in the Western tradition, the great originator of games of luck.
insights.locator: But then if you can’t afford the trip to Delphi

insights.claim: The second Greek risk-mitigation technique was making offerings to establish a benign relationship with the gods by signifying subordination and attempting to read their intentions.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Managing the sentiment of an unaccountable power is an ancient strategy — and still describes how markets position around policymakers.
insights.locator: But the other way of mitigating risk

themes.theme: Central bank independence as the sirens myth

insights.claim: Central bank independence is a self-binding and credible-commitment problem in which depriving yourself of freedom is the way to better achieve your goals, because what central banks want is to establish a credible reliable reaction function.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Independence is valuable precisely because it removes optionality — any policy change that restores discretion mechanically degrades commitment value.
insights.quote: They want to make themselves into a function. And to do that, they have to deprive themselves of freedom.
insights.locator: Yeah, I think the general problem is that of self-binding

insights.claim: The Odysseus-and-the-sirens framing of central banking is explicitly a conservative myth, in which the siren song is the blandishments of democratic politics demanding short-term fixes.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Naming the metaphor as ideological reframes the independence debate as a political choice rather than a technical necessity — a lens for reading attacks on the Fed.
insights.quote: this is a conservative myth, by the way
insights.locator: And the temptations, in the case, of political economy

insights.claim: The failure chain from indulging political short-termism runs first through destabilization of expectations and, with continued indulgence, ends in hyperinflation.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Expectations de-anchoring is the leading indicator; hyperinflation is the terminal state — watch breakevens rather than headline CPI for regime breaks.
insights.locator: the result would be a destabilization of expectations

insights.claim: A purely mechanical nondiscretionary Taylor-rule central bank would deliver the same commitment without the drama, but central banking's value partly lies in being visibly seen to resist the easy option as a person rather than a robot.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Credibility is partly performative — which is why leadership personality at the Fed moves markets more than any rule-based model predicts.
insights.quote: whereas the drama of central banking, in some senses, is to resist the thing that will be easy and to be seen to be resisting it
insights.locator: But that would also deprive you of the drama

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the Fed, is against forward guidance, putting the softer 'Delphic' model of central banking — a data-driven negotiated conversation in which the central bank acts as a participating forecaster — back into contention.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A Fed chair hostile to forward guidance means less pre-committed path information and higher rate-path volatility around each meeting.
insights.quote: The Delphic vision is a little bit more like the forward-guidance-type story that is now so much in debate because [Kevin] Warsh, the new chair of the Fed, is against it.
insights.locator: And what’s interesting is there’s another type of model

insights.claim: Central banks operate under two competing archetypes — the Odyssean rock-like figure tied down and bent on its course regardless, versus the Delphic oracle that answers questions and reads omens as a participating forecaster.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A clean two-mode taxonomy for classifying any central bank communication regime and its implied volatility profile.
insights.locator: And the central bank becomes a sort of participating forecaster
